question: After Rome, which fats survive where — and what do cooks, monks and herders keep going?
summary: This is the thinnest folio in the program because the evidence thins. In Baghdad's tenth-century cookbook, meat is fried in rendered sheep's tail fat and cold dishes are dressed with olive oil ([[e1]]); in western Europe the monasteries and cathedrals keep an oil culture alive for rites and diet in a world of butter and lard ([[b1]]); in Anglo-Saxon England butter is a lord's luxury from sheep's milk, and in Ireland butter is buried in bogs ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]).

The east moves on. Tamil texts of the 600s–700s describe the sesame press, the *chekku* ([[ec3]]); late-Tang farm calendars list pressing seeds for oil as a fourth-month task ([[te1]]); monasteries keep an ever-burning oil lamp ([[b2]]); and the Tang pharmacopoeias rank milk, soured milk, su and ghee-like ti hu as the stages of the soul ([[b3]]). Soap is already a craft in Italy ([[ec4]]), and Norsemen hunt whales and walrus ([[ec5]]).

themes.title: Oil in the northern fat world
text: Olive oil is carried across the break by the church, by cooks of the Near East, and by Italian soap-makers.

themes.title: Butter at the Atlantic edge
text: Sheep's butter as a thane's luxury; bog butter hidden against raiders or kept cool.

themes.title: Asia presses on
text: The Tamil press, the Tang pressing calendar, the lamp offering and the Buddhist ladder from milk to ghee show fat as both commodity and symbol.

themes.title: First whalers
text: Ohthere's voyage and North Sea whaling are the prelude to the Basque industry of the next folio.

turning_points.text: Monasteries keep an oil culture alive in the north.
The Tamil chekku presses sesame oil.
The Tang pharmacopoeia ranks milk, lo, su and ti hu as the stages of the soul.
The Baghdad cookbook: tail fat in the pot, olive oil on the cold dishes.

how_to_read: With only ten entries the folio reads best straight through. Several dates are ranges for ‘the early Middle Ages’ because the sources do not narrow them.
The next folio is where documents (customs, Lent rules, Geniza ledgers, whale taxes) make fats countable.

sources.intro: A thin and uneven record: a translated Baghdad cookbook, a popular history of butter, Achaya and Needham for Asia, and Mueller, Ward and Ellis for Europe.
main: Nasrallah's translation of Ibn Sayyar for Baghdad ([[e1]]); Needham and Kieschnick for the Tang entries ([[te1]], [[b2]], [[b3]]).
Achaya for the Tamil press ([[ec3]]); Khosrova for butter ([[ec1]], [[ec2]]); Ward for soap ([[ec4]]); Ellis for whaling ([[ec5]]).
contested: Mueller's monastic ‘islands of oil’ cite no councils ([[b1]]).
The thousand-year-old Irish butter is a museum label as reported ([[ec2]]).
Italian soap-making is dated only as ‘the early Middle Ages’ ([[ec4]]).
gaps: The Islamic agricultural writers and Watson's thesis (now much criticised) are not covered; Andalusian and Sicilian olive oil are missing.
No source for Carolingian fats, or for African and American oil crops.
